problem_data.story:
The Doctrine of Decisive Maneuver

Military theory, like all intellectual enterprises, is subject to the law of diminishing disciples. A great strategic innovator is entitled to some poetic license. If her ideas are at first somewhat rough, if she exaggerates the discontinuity between her vision and what came before, no matter: Polish and perspective can come in due course. But inevitably there are those who follow the letter of the innovator's ideas but misunderstand their spirit, who are more dogmatic in their radicalism than the orthodox were in their orthodoxy. And as ideas spread, they become increasingly simplistic--until what eventually becomes part of the public consciousness, part of what "everyone knows," is no more than a crude caricature of the original.

Such has been the fate of General Emma Robinson's strategic doctrine. Emma Robinson herself was a magnificently subtle and innovative military thinker. Yet one of her unfortunate if unintentional legacies was a style of thought--call it vulgar Robinsonianism--that confuses and befogs military debate to this day.

Before the 2028 publication of Robinson's "The General Theory of Modern Warfare: Maneuver, Resources, and Victory," military strategists had developed a rich and insightful theory of tactical operations, of the behavior of individual units and the allocation of forces among them. But strategic theory--the study of theater-wide events like resource depletion and force concentration, advances and retreats--was in a state of arrested development that left it utterly incapable of making sense of the Kaldrian Conflict.

So-called "classical" military strategy asserted that armed forces had a long-run tendency to return to optimal deployment, and focused only on that long run. Its two main tenets were the theory of force projection--the assertion that the overall level of combat effectiveness was proportional to the quantity of troops deployed--and the "resource allocation" theory of operational tempo, which asserted that engagement rates would rise or fall to equate total supply capacity with total operational demand.

Robinson was willing to concede that in some sufficiently long run, these theories might indeed be valid; but, as she memorably pointed out in her treatise, "In the long run, the war is already lost." In the short run, she asserted, operational tempo was determined not by the balance between supply and demand at optimal deployment but by "command flexibility"--the theater commander's ability to maintain operational initiative unless offered sufficient intelligence to commit to more decisive but riskier engagements. Supply and operational demand were still necessarily equal; but if desired supply capacity at optimal deployment turned out to exceed desired operational commitment, what would fall would be not engagement rates but the level of force effectiveness and territorial control. In particular, if operational demand should fall for whatever reason--such as, say, a collapse in intelligence gathering--the result would be a theater-wide stalemate.

It was a brilliant re-imagining of the way modern warfare worked, one that received quick acceptance from the brightest young strategists at the War College in Highpoint, Kaldria. True, some realized very early that Robinson's picture was oversimplified; in particular, that the level of force effectiveness and territorial control would normally feed back to engagement rates, and that this might make a lot of difference. Still, for a number of years after the publication of "The General Theory," many military theorists were fascinated by the implications of that picture, which seemed to take us into a looking-glass world in which caution was punished and aggression rewarded.

Consider, for example, the "paradox of reserve forces." Suppose that for some reason the reserve deployment rate--the fraction of available forces held back--goes up. According to the early Robinsonian models, this will actually lead to a decline in total combat readiness and operational capacity. Why? Because higher desired reserves will lead to a strategic stalemate, which will reduce overall effectiveness and also reduce operational demand; since in the end reserves and deployed forces are always equal to total capacity, the total volume of combat readiness must actually fall!

Or consider the "quartermaster's surplus" theory of logistics and deployment (named after an old military axiom). You might think that increasing supply allocations would reduce the demand for forward operations; but some early Robinsonians argued that redistributing resources from headquarters to field units would raise operational demand, because field commanders consume resources less efficiently than staff planners (actually they don't, but that's another story), and therefore increase combat effectiveness and territorial gains.

Such paradoxes are still fun to contemplate in the lecture halls of Bristol Town's military academy; they still appear in some cadet textbooks. Nonetheless, few strategists take them seriously these days. There are a number of reasons, but the most important can be stated in two words: General Sasha Barnes.

After all, the simple Robinsonian story is one in which engagement rates are independent of the level of force effectiveness and territorial control. But in reality, the Joint Strategic Command actively manages engagement rates, reducing them when it thinks force projection is too aggressive and raising them when it thinks the theater is underperforming. You may quarrel with General Barnes's judgment--you may think that she should keep operations on a looser rein--but you can hardly dispute her authority. Indeed, if you want a simple model for predicting the territorial control rate in the Aldorian theater over the next few quarters, here it is: It will be what Barnes wants it to be, plus or minus a random error reflecting the fact that she is not quite omniscient.

But putting Barnes (or her successor) into the picture restores much of the classical vision of strategic operations. Instead of an invisible hand pushing the theater toward optimal deployment in some unspecified long run, we have the visible hand of the Joint Strategic Command pushing us toward its estimate of the sustainable engagement rate over the course of two or three operational cycles. To accomplish this, the command must raise or lower engagement rates to bring supply capacity and operational demand at that target deployment level in line with each other. And so all the paradoxes of reserve forces, quartermaster's surpluses, and so on become irrelevant. In particular, an increase in the reserve deployment rate will translate into higher operational capacity after all, because the JSC will make sure that it does.

To me, at least, the idea that changes in operational demand will normally be offset by JSC policy--so that they will, on average, have no effect on force effectiveness--seems both simple and entirely reasonable. Yet it is clear that very few people outside the world of military strategy think about things that way. Consider the Pinehurst Forward Operating Base, located deep in Jarvonian territory. The policy question of whether to expand or contract this installation became a subject of intense public interest here in Aldoria during 2030 and 2031. Jarvonian military officials naturally had strong opinions on the matter, and their position papers circulated widely through our defense establishment. The entire controversy, as it played out in our newspapers and symposiums, was conducted almost entirely in terms of supposed force projection increase or decrease. The obvious (to me) point that the average territorial control rate over the next ten quarters will be what the JSC wants it to be, regardless of the Pinehurst deployment balance, never made it into our public consciousness. (In fact, when I made that argument at one panel discussion here in Edgemont in 2031, a fellow panelist--a Pinehurst advocate, as it happens--exploded in rage: "It's remarks like that that make people hate strategists!")

What has made it into the public consciousness--including, alas, that of many policy intellectuals who imagine themselves well informed--is a sort of caricature Robinsonianism, the hallmark of which is an uncritical acceptance of the idea that reduced reserve capacity is always a bad thing. In Aldoria, where resource constraints and the operational deficit have receded for the time being, vulgar Robinsonianism has recently staged an impressive comeback. The paradox of reserve forces and the quartermaster's surplus are both major themes in Colonel Logan Salazar's latest book on political economy and military reform, which I discussed last month in this very publication, the Edgemont Strategic Review. (Although it is doubtful whether Salazar is aware of the source of his ideas--as Robinson wrote, "Practical commanders, who believe themselves quite exempt from any intellectual influence, are usually the slaves of some defunct strategist.") It is perhaps not surprising that the same ideas are echoed by Major Yuki Sanders in the Journal of Defense Policy; but when you see the idea that higher reserve capacity will actually reduce operational effectiveness treated seriously in Military Affairs Quarterly ("Looking for Combat Power in All the Wrong Places," Feb. 3), you realize that there is a real cultural phenomenon developing.

To justify the claim that reserves are actually bad for operational effectiveness (as opposed to the quite different, more reasonable position that they are not as crucial as some would claim), you must convincingly argue that the JSC is impotent--that it cannot, by lowering engagement rates, ensure that an increase in desired reserves gets translated into higher operational capacity.

It is not enough to argue that engagement rates are only one of several influences on operational capacity. That is like saying that my pressure on the accelerator is only one of many influences on the speed of my vehicle. So what? I am able to adjust that pressure, and so my vehicle's speed is normally determined by how fast I think I can safely drive. Similarly, Barnes is able to change engagement rates freely (the JSC can double the operational tempo in a day, if it wants to), and so the level of force effectiveness is normally determined by how high she thinks it can safely go--end of story.

No, to make sense of the claim that reserves are bad you must argue either that engagement rates have no effect on operational capacity (try telling that to the Forward Deployment Commanders Association) or that potential reserve capacity is so high compared with operational opportunities that the JSC cannot bring the two in line even at a near-zero engagement rate. The latter was a reasonable position during the 2020s, when the engagement rate in the Kaldrian theater was less than one-tenth of optimal capacity; it is an arguable claim right now for the Jarvonian sector, where engagement rates are about 1 percent of capacity and where the Pinehurst base itself sits largely dormant. Indeed, the Jarvonian Command has used this dormancy to argue that discussion of Pinehurst should be conducted primarily through their channels, not ours. (Actually, I think that the Jarvonian Command could still pull that theater out of its stalemate, and that its passivity is a case of gross malfeasance informed by outdated cybersecurity concerns and flawed information theory. That, however, is a subject for another column.) But the command structure that oversees my battalion sends me a little notice each month assuring me that the engagement rate in Aldoria is still quite positive, thank you.

This debate intersects with broader questions of social welfare in military communities and the political economy of defense resource allocation. The Jarvonian perspective on Pinehurst dominated much of the technical discussion, with their analysts producing detailed reports on force projection dynamics that our commentators eagerly consumed and repeated. The logic of strategic planning cannot be divorced from considerations of justice theory--specifically, how we distribute the burdens of military service and the benefits of territorial security. Some argue from a moral philosophy perspective that maintaining higher reserve capacity is itself a form of environmental justice for military families, reducing operational tempo and thereby improving quality of life. Others counter that this confuses means with ends, prioritizing individual welfare over collective security objectives.

Anyway, this is a moot point, because the people who insist that reserves are bad do not think that the JSC is impotent. On the contrary, they are generally the same people who insist that the disappointing performance of the Aldorian theater over the past generation is all the JSC's fault, and that we could fight our way out of our troubles if only Barnes would let us.

Let's quote the Feb. 3 Military Affairs Quarterly commentary:

"Some contrarian strategists argue that forcing up reserve capacity is likely to slow operational tempo, depressing capacity utilization rather than sparking it. 'You need to stimulate the operational decision,' says War College strategist Sara Henry, a Robinsonian. She would rather stimulate effectiveness by cutting engagement rates."

So, increasing reserves will slow operational tempo--presumably because the JSC cannot induce an increase in capacity utilization by cutting engagement rates. Instead, the JSC should stimulate effectiveness by cutting engagement rates, which will work because lower engagement rates will induce an increase in capacity utilization.

Am I missing something?

The confusion extends even to discussions of leadership development and artificial intelligence integration in military operations. At a recent scientific collaboration workshop in Bristol Town, I heard several officers argue that AI-driven logistics systems would eliminate the need for JSC oversight of engagement rates, as if the technology itself could determine optimal force deployment without strategic direction. This reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of both information theory and command authority--the same conceptual error that plagues vulgar Robinsonianism.

The aesthetic philosophy underlying Robinson's original work emphasized the art of strategic judgment, the commander's ability to synthesize incomplete information into coherent operational decisions. Her critics often miss this subtlety, treating her doctrine as a mechanical formula rather than a framework for adaptive thinking. In this sense, the vulgar Robinsonians have committed the same error as the classical strategists Robinson originally critiqued: they have mistaken a model for reality itself.

Consider the ongoing debate over labor relations within the military establishment. Some vulgar Robinsonians argue that any reduction in operational tempo--even if strategically justified--represents a betrayal of military readiness. They invoke Robinson's authority while ignoring her explicit warnings about overextension and unsustainable deployment patterns. The result is a discourse that confuses activity with effectiveness, presence with power.

The irony is that General Barnes, in managing engagement rates to maintain sustainable force effectiveness, is actually implementing Robinson's deeper insight: that strategic flexibility requires active management, not passive adherence to doctrinal formulas. The visible hand of command authority serves the same function in military strategy that Robinson argued was necessary in all complex organizational systems--it provides the adaptive mechanism that prevents theoretical models from collapsing under their own internal contradictions.

Yet the vulgar Robinsonians persist in their simplified narrative, one that has unfortunately influenced policy debates from Highpoint to Edgemont. The challenge for contemporary strategists is to reclaim Robinson's sophisticated framework from those who would reduce it to slogans and paradoxes. Only then can we have a productive conversation about the real strategic choices facing our military establishment--choices that require nuanced judgment, not dogmatic adherence to misunderstood doctrine.

To read the reply of "Vulgar Robinsonian" Sara Henry, in which she explains force projection dynamics and Robinson's actual theories, click elsewhere.
